47: ## 1. System & Architecture Overview
48: 
49: [`Project.MM/LocalConfig`](.) contains a fully self-contained local simulation setup for an **ESP32-based Embedded Network Attached Storage (NAS) and Static Web Server**. Designed for the `CSE0611324` Microprocessor & Microcontrollers laboratory curriculum, it runs completely on your workstation without cloud dependencies or upload rate limits.
50: 
51: ```
52:                       +---------------------------------------------------+
53:                       |               Host Workstation                    |
54:                       |   VS Code + PlatformIO + Wokwi Simulator Engine   |
55:                       +-------------------------+-------------------------+
56:                                                 |
57:                                     ws://localhost:9011
58:                                                 |
59:                                                 ▼
60:                                     +-----------------------+
61:                                     |     wokwigw.exe       |
62:                                     | (Listens: 0.0.0.0:9080)|
63:                                     +-----------+-----------+
64:                                                 |
65:                          +----------------------+----------------------+
66:                          |                                             |
67:                          ▼                                             ▼
68:             [Wired Ethernet Interface]                    [Windows Mobile Hotspot]
69:              IP: e.g., 192.168.1.105                        Virtual IP: 192.168.137.1
70:                          |                                             |
71:                          ▼                                             ▼
72:             Lab Workstations / PCs                       Smartphones & Tablets
73: ```
74: 
75: ### 1.1 Embedded Hardware Architecture
76: * **Target Microcontroller**: Classic ESP32 DevKit V1 powered by the Xtensa Dual-Core 32-bit LX6 microprocessor operating at 240 MHz, with 520 KB on-chip SRAM.
77: * **Storage Medium**: Hardware VSPI-driven MicroSD Card module formatted with standard FAT32 block storage.
78: * **Firmware Framework**: Native Arduino-ESP32 core (`WebServer.h`, `SD.h`, `SPI.h`, `WiFi.h`).
79:

744: ## 9. Evaluator Q&A Defense (Anticipated Questions & Rebuttals)
745: 
746: ### Q1: Why ESP32 instead of a Raspberry Pi?
747: - **Cost**: An ESP32 is \$4, whereas a Raspberry Pi 4 is \$45 to \$75.
748: - **Power Consumption**: ESP32 consumes 80 mA to 150 mA at 3.3V (<0.5 Watt). A Raspberry Pi draws 3 to 7 Watts. An ESP32 can run for weeks on a standard 18650 lithium battery.
749: - **Boot Time**: ESP32 boots in less than 500 milliseconds. A Raspberry Pi takes 25 to 45 seconds to boot Linux.
750: - **Security**: There is no underlying Linux OS, no open SSH ports, no shell vulnerabilities, and no kernel root exploits.
751: 
752: ---
753: 
754: ### Q2: What happens if an uploaded file exceeds the ESP32 RAM?
755: - **Rebuttal**: Our upload architecture never buffers the entire file in RAM. It uses the `server.upload()` streaming multipart parser. Incoming TCP packets are received in small slices (up to 1,436 bytes) and accumulated into a **512-byte single-sector buffer** before flushing to the MicroSD card via `CMD24` (`WRITE_BLOCK_SINGLE`). As a result, the RAM footprint remains fixed at approximately **~2 KB** of heap memory regardless of whether transferring a 10 KB assembly program or a 50 MB binary image.
756: 
757: ---
758: 
759: ### Q3: Can this simulation firmware run on real, physical hardware?
760: - **Rebuttal**: **Yes, 100% without code changes.**
761:   The pins used (`GPIO 5`, `GPIO 18`, `GPIO 19`, `GPIO 23`) are the exact standard hardware VSPI pins of the ESP32 DevKit V1. If you wire a physical MicroSD breakout module to those pins and flash this firmware, the only change needed is replacing the SSID `"Wokwi-GUEST"` with your local home or university Wi-Fi network name.
762: 
763: ---
764: 
765: ### Q4: Why SPI mode for the SD card instead of 4-bit SDMMC?
766: - **Rebuttal**: While 4-bit SDMMC offers higher bandwidth, it requires 6 specific dedicated pins (including GPIO 12, which is an internal strapping pin that can brick bootup if pulled high at power-on). SPI mode requires only 4 pins, has universal compatibility across all SD and MicroSD breakout boards, and provides plenty of bandwidth for low-power edge NAS operations.
767: 
768: ---
769: 
770: ### Q5: How does the web server avoid blocking other background tasks?
771: - **Rebuttal**: We take advantage of the ESP32's dual-core Xtensa architecture and the FreeRTOS real-time operating system. Time-critical background operations (like sensor telemetry or network health tests) are pinned to Core 1 using `xTaskCreatePinnedToCore`, while the networking stack runs independently on Core 0.
772: 
773: ---
774: 
775: ### Q6: Does the file server only work on localhost, or can other network devices connect?
776: - **Rebuttal**: It is fully accessible across the entire local network through three distinct deployment topologies:
777:   1. **Deterministic Hotspot**: Enabling Windows Mobile Hotspot assigns the host PC `192.168.137.1`. Any smartphone or laptop connecting to the hotspot accesses `http://192.168.137.1:9080/` with zero router dependencies.
778:   2. **Shared Wireless Wi-Fi (All-Wireless)**: Both the host PC and external mobile devices connect wirelessly to the same Wi-Fi router. Clients navigate to `http://<HOST_WIFI_IP>:9080/` without any physical cables.
779:   3. **Wired Campus LAN Switch**: Lab PCs on the same Ethernet switch access the server at `http://<HOST_ETHERNET_IP>:9080/`.
780:   4. **Physical Silicon**: On real hardware, the ESP32 either connects to the local router or broadcasts its own autonomous SoftAP (`192.168.4.1`), serving all network clients on standard port 80 with no host computer required.
781: 
782: ---
783: 
784: ### Q7: Why did Wokwi Cloud show a paywall, and how does your project bypass it?
785: - **Rebuttal**: Wokwi Cloud's free tier provides a Public Gateway that only supports outbound NAT requests (e.g. hitting weather APIs), but blocks inbound TCP connections from external desktop browsers unless subscribing to their paid Private Gateway ($7–$15/mo). We bypassed this in two ways:
786:   1. For cloud users, [`Project.MM/CloudConfig`](https://github.com/b1tranger/Microprocessor_Assembly_Lab/blob/main/Project.MM/CloudConfig) uses an internal FreeRTOS loopback client (`runClientTests` on `127.0.0.1`) that tests all endpoints 100% for free inside the simulator.
787:   2. For full interactive browser testing, [`Project.MM/LocalConfig`](https://github.com/b1tranger/Microprocessor_Assembly_Lab/blob/main/Project.MM/LocalConfig) runs locally in VS Code with the free community license and local `wokwigw.exe` bridge.
788:

791: ### Q8: Why choose Classic ESP32 with SPI over an ESP32-S3 with a USB flash drive?
792: - **Rebuttal**: The Classic ESP32 (WROOM-32) with a SPI MicroSD module costs under 400 BDT, is ubiquitously available, has a mature, rock-solid Arduino `SD` library, and aligns 100% with the pinout table submitted in our course proposal (`GPIO 5, 18, 19, 23`). While the ESP32-S3 supports native USB host for pen drives, it requires complex USB MSC drivers and different pin configurations.
793: 
794: ---
795: 
796: ### Q9: How would this system operate in a field environment without an internet router?
797: - **Rebuttal**: The ESP32 natively supports **Soft Access Point (SoftAP) Mode** (`WiFi.softAP()`). In an off-grid forest or disaster zone, the ESP32 broadcasts its own Wi-Fi SSID (`"ESP32-Edge-NAS"`). Field personnel connect their smartphones directly to the ESP32 and access files at `http://192.168.4.1/` without needing an internet connection, external router, or PC.
798: 
799: ---
800: 
801: ### Q10: How does this system compare to LocalSend / LocalSend Web?
802: - **Rebuttal**: LocalSend's "Share via Browser" (Web Share) mode turns a desktop PC into a temporary web server on the local network so other machines can transfer files in a browser without installing the app. Our project provides that exact same zero-install browser experience for lab computers. However, from an embedded systems perspective, `Project.MM` is fundamentally distinct: it runs on a \$4 ESP32 microcontroller with 520 KB SRAM rather than a multi-gigabyte PC OS, writes files across hardware VSPI lines directly into FAT32 MicroSD card sectors with a strict ~2 KB RAM streaming overhead, and acts as an autonomous hardware appliance that does not depend on a host PC remaining online.
803: 
804: ---
805: 
806: ### Q11: How do you handle campus Wi-Fi AP/Client Isolation during a lab demonstration?
807: - **Rebuttal**: University routers and enterprise switches often enforce AP/Client Isolation to prevent peer-to-peer communication between connected devices. To guarantee that our live demonstration is never blocked by institutional firewall policies, we activate **Windows Mobile Hotspot** on the host workstation. Windows configures a virtual NAT gateway at `192.168.137.1`. Any smartphone or lab computer connecting to this hotspot can reach `http://192.168.137.1:9080/` with zero router restrictions.
808: 
809: ---
810: 
811: ### Q12: Why is the dashboard styled with sharp geometry (border-radius: 0) and no animated status dot?
812: - **Rebuttal**: In professional high-density engineering appliances and telemetry consoles, curved borders introduce unnecessary visual noise and table misalignment. By establishing a strict `border-radius: 0 !important;` rule and removing distracting pulsating online badges, the interface emphasizes immediate data density, high-contrast monospace technical readability, and modern matte aesthetics.
813: 
814: ---
815: 
816: ### Q13: Why did uploads stay stuck at 100% for several seconds before completing?
817: - **Rebuttal**: In our simulation architecture, client uploads traverse the host machine's loopback interface at gigabit speed, filling the OS socket buffer almost immediately so `xhr.upload.onprogress` reaches 100% in milliseconds. However, the virtual ESP32 runs at cycle-accurate simulation speed, bit-banging and clocking each 512-byte sector across the simulated VSPI bus into the virtual FAT32 SD card. In the web UI, we introduced a dedicated commit transition state (`Writing to Storage`, `⚡ Committing...`, `⏱ Finalizing SD card write`) to explicitly inform users that network delivery has finished and the simulated microcontroller is actively committing blocks to storage.
818: 
819: ---
820: 
821: ### Q14: How does your firmware guarantee zero corrupted or 0-byte files if an upload is interrupted?
822: - **Rebuttal**: In `handleFileUpload()`, on `UPLOAD_FILE_ABORTED` or on write error detection, the firmware immediately closes the active file handle and invokes `SD.remove(currentUploadTarget)`. Furthermore, the POST completion callback strictly verifies `upload.status == UPLOAD_FILE_END && upload.totalSize > 0 && !uploadWriteError`; otherwise, it returns HTTP 500 JSON error. This ensures aborted uploads never linger as empty 0-byte entries on FAT32.
823: 
824: ---
825: 
826: ### Q15: Why is the SPI clock initialized to 4 MHz rather than 25 MHz or 40 MHz?
827: - **Rebuttal**: Virtual SD card simulation in Wokwi (as well as physical Dupont jumper wires on breadboards) suffers from timing signal degradation when clocking bulk data block writes (`CMD24`/`CMD25`) above 10 MHz, causing `FR_DISK_ERR` and stream write failures. Standard 4 MHz SPI provides 100% block write reliability without clock jitter in both virtual simulation and physical hardware prototyping.

831: ### Q16: How does the asset generation pipeline allow web developers to modify HTML without editing C++ code?
832: - **Rebuttal**: Frontend files exist as standard HTML/CSS/JS in `Project.MM/LocalConfig/data/www/` (`fileserver.html`, `index.html`), which can be edited and previewed directly in web browsers. Our build script [`refresh_firmware.ps1`](https://github.com/b1tranger/Microprocessor_Assembly_Lab/blob/main/Project.MM/LocalConfig/refresh_firmware.ps1) (and its companion `refresh_firmware.bat`) automatically runs `scripts/generate_assets.ps1` to convert all web assets into PROGMEM byte arrays in `include/default_assets.h` before invoking PlatformIO. Developers never need to manually escape HTML strings inside C++ files.
833: 
834: ---
835: 
836: ### Q17: Why use HTTP and not HTTPS (TLS/SSL)?
837: - **Rebuttal**:
838:   1. **RAM Overhead of TLS**: Establishing a single TLS 1.2/1.3 session via `mbedTLS` on ESP32 consumes **45 KB to 65 KB of internal SRAM** for asymmetric cipher state machines, session keys, and certificate chain buffers. On an ESP32 with ~320 KB accessible user heap, handling multiple concurrent HTTPS connections quickly causes heap fragmentation and socket starvation (`ENOMEM`).
839:   2. **Cryptographic Computation Bottleneck**: Microcontroller CPUs lack dedicated hardware acceleration for high-entropy asymmetric public-key handshakes (RSA 2048/4096 or ECDSA), introducing multi-second connection latencies and dropping streaming transfer throughput below 150 KB/s.
840:   3. **Air-Gapped & Local LAN Boundary**: `Project.MM` is designed as an air-gapped edge appliance for isolated subnets, emergency off-grid nodes, and local Wi-Fi networks protected by physical layer security (WPA2/WPA3 enterprise Wi-Fi or direct peer-to-peer SoftAP). Traffic never crosses public internet routing hops.
841:   4. **Self-Signed Certificate Friction**: In local IP deployments (`192.168.x.x`), HTTPS requires self-signed certificates, which cause modern smartphone and desktop browsers to throw intrusive security warning interstitials ("Your connection is not private") that disrupt zero-install field access.
842:   5. **Enterprise Architecture Pattern**: In production deployments requiring WAN access, embedded engineers place the ESP32 behind an edge reverse proxy (such as Nginx, Caddy, or Cloudflare Tunnel) on the router or gateway. The proxy handles public TLS termination, while the ESP32 remains lean, ultra-responsive, and dedicated to raw SPI/FAT32 I/O.
843: 
844: ---
845: 
846: ### Q18: Why is storage capped at 256 MB in simulation, and does this limit apply to real hardware?
847: - **Rebuttal**:
848:   1. **Wokwi Simulation Engine Limit**: In Wokwi for VS Code and Wokwi CLI, **`256M` is the hardcoded upper capacity limit** for the virtual `wokwi-microsd-card` component (the default is 8 MB, and the maximum configurable value in `wokwi.toml` is 256 MB). Attempting values like `512M` or `1G` throws a simulator validation error.
849:   2. **Host Startup & Writeback Performance**: In simulation, Wokwi formats the virtual disk into host RAM upon boot and writes modified sectors back to `data/network/` on your SSD when stopped. Keeping the virtual disk at 256 MB guarantees near-instant simulation boot times (< 2 seconds) and rapid file synchronization.
850:   3. **Zero Limit on Physical Silicon**: **This limit does NOT exist on physical hardware.** The ESP32 Arduino FAT32 driver (`SD.h` / FatFs) standardly supports physical SDHC MicroSD cards up to **32 GB** (and exFAT/FAT32 formatted cards up to **128 GB - 2 TB** with standard 32 KB cluster allocation).
851: 
852: ---
853: 
854: ### Q19: This is a simulation, but what would be the configurations in a real-life project? What are the bare minimum and maximum settings for ESP32?
855: - **Rebuttal**:
856:   - **Bare Minimum Real-World Hardware & Firmware Configuration (Ultra-Low Cost & Field Battery Node)**:
857:     - **Microcontroller**: Classic ESP32-WROOM-32 (240 MHz dual-core Xtensa LX6, 520 KB internal SRAM, 4 MB external SPI Flash). Under-clockable to **80 MHz or 160 MHz** via `setCpuFrequencyMhz()` to drop power consumption to < 35 mA.
858:     - **RAM Footprint**: Static firmware allocation ~38 KB; fixed **~2 KB streaming memory window** using our 512-byte sector-aligned buffer for file transfers.
859:     - **Physical Storage**: Standard 1 GB to 4 GB Class 4/10 MicroSD card formatted with FAT32 (512-byte physical sectors).
860:     - **Hardware Interface**: Hardware VSPI (`GPIO 18` SCK, `GPIO 19` MISO, `GPIO 23` MOSI, `GPIO 5` CS) with standard 10k pull-up resistors on MISO/MOSI, clocked at 4 MHz to 10 MHz.
861:     - **Power Supply**: Single 3.7V 18650 Lithium-ion cell (2600 mAh) paired with a TP4056 charge controller and a low-dropout 3.3V regulator (e.g. ME6211 or AMS1117-3.3 capable of 500 mA peak Wi-Fi TX bursts).
862:     - **Network**: Autonomous SoftAP mode (`WiFi.softAP("ESP32-Edge-NAS")`) serving clients at default gateway `http://192.168.4.1/` with zero router or internet connection required.
863:   - **Maximum / High-Performance Real-World Configuration (Enterprise Industrial Edge NAS)**:
864:     - **Microcontroller**: ESP32-S3-WROOM-2 or ESP32-WROVER-E with **8 MB to 16 MB Octal PSRAM** and **16 MB to 32 MB Quad/Octal SPI Flash** running at full 240 MHz.
865:     - **Physical Storage**: High-endurance 32 GB to 64 GB SanDisk/Samsung Extreme UHS-I MicroSD card.
866:     - **Hardware Interface**: **4-bit SDMMC Hardware Mode** (`SD_MMC.h` utilizing 4 data lines: `D0-D3`, `CLK`, `CMD`), clocked at **40 MHz to 50 MHz**. This increases real-world read/write bandwidth from ~1.2 MB/s (SPI) to **10 MB/s - 15 MB/s**. Alternatively, on the ESP32-S3, native USB 2.0 OTG Host mode (`USBHost.h`) can mount external USB thumb drives or external SSDs directly.
867:     - **Concurrency & OS**: FreeRTOS multi-core pinned tasks: Core 0 handles lwIP network protocol processing and high-throughput TCP windowing; Core 1 handles asynchronous non-blocking WebServer routes, multipart FAT32 chunking, and WebSocket telemetry push.
868:     - **Power Optimization**: Dynamic Frequency Scaling (DFS) with automatic modem sleep when idle, and deep-sleep current draw under **15 $\mu$A** during inactivity, waking up via capacitive touch or PIR motion sensor.
869: 
870: ---

872: ### Q20: Why did 4KB buffering fail with `Sector write failed: 0 / 4096 bytes written`, and how does 512-byte single-sector alignment solve it?
873: - **Rebuttal**:
874:   1. **The Multi-Sector Rejection (`ACMD23` / `CMD25`)**: The physical sector size of standard FAT32 micro-SD cards is strictly 512 bytes. When 4,096 bytes (8 sectors) were written via `uploadFile.write()`, FatFs passed `count = 8` to `sd_diskio.cpp`. When `count > 1`, the driver dispatches `sdWriteSectors()`, which issues `ACMD23` (`SET_WR_BLK_ERASE_COUNT`) to pre-erase sectors before sending `CMD25` (`WRITE_BLOCK_MULTIPLE`).
875:   2. **Simulator & SPI Hardware Limitation**: Wokwi's virtual SD component (as well as many budget physical SPI micro-SD breakout boards) does not implement `ACMD23` in SPI mode. The virtual SD controller returns an illegal command token (`0x04`), causing `sdTransaction` to abort before writing anything and returning 0 bytes written.
876:   3. **The 512-Byte Single-Sector Solution**: Setting `#define UPLOAD_SECTOR_BUFFER_SIZE 512` forces every disk write to equal exactly one physical sector (`count == 1`). This routes execution to `sdWriteSector()`, which issues standard **`CMD24` (`WRITE_BLOCK_SINGLE`)** with token `0xFE`. `CMD24` never issues `ACMD23` or `CMD25` and is 100% universally supported across Wokwi virtual media, budget SPI breakout boards, and physical silicon.
877: 
878: ---
879: 
880: ### Q21: How does the ESP32 file server handle concurrent client requests, FreeRTOS tasks, and socket starvation?
881: - **Rebuttal**:
882:   1. **Dual-Core FreeRTOS Separation**: Core 0 is dedicated to the lwIP TCP/IP stack and RF modulation. Core 1 runs the Arduino `loop()` which drives `server.handleClient()`.
883:   2. **Synchronous Multipart Streaming**: The `WebServer` multipart parser reads TCP payload chunks sequentially inside `handleFileUpload()`. File writing is strictly synchronous and sector-buffered, preventing multiple requests from clobbering the active `File` handle.
884:   3. **Socket Hygiene & Cooperative Yielding**: Background diagnostic threads (`runClientTests` on Core 1) use `performTestRequest()` with explicit stream draining (`stream->read()`) into a dummy buffer and a `vTaskDelay(800 / portTICK_PERIOD_MS)` cooperative yield. This gives `server.handleClient()` dedicated CPU cycles to finalize TCP `FIN/ACK` handshakes, completely eliminating socket starvation and connection resets (`-11`).
885:   4. **Abort Purge Circuit Breaker**: If a client disconnects mid-upload (`UPLOAD_FILE_ABORTED`), the firmware immediately closes the handle and calls `SD.remove(currentUploadTarget)`, guaranteeing zero corrupted or empty 0-byte ghost files on flash media.
886: 
887: ---
888: 
889: ### Q22: Why were file details hidden on mobile browsers after selection, and how does your responsive UI resolve it?
890: - **Rebuttal**:
891:   1. **Mobile File Input Limitations**: On mobile devices (Android Chrome, iOS Safari), standard `<input type="file">` elements render a 100%-width system button (`Choose file`). Because of narrow viewports and aggressive browser text truncation, chosen filenames are rendered with ellipses (`IMG-202...`) or hidden completely, leaving users with zero confirmation of what file was selected.
892:   2. **Dedicated Monospace Preview Card (`.file-detail-card`)**: We implemented an industrial-styled preview card that dynamically un-hides via JavaScript upon the `change` DOM event. It displays:
893:      - The complete sanitized filename with monospace formatting and ellipsis text protection.
894:      - An exact formatted file size badge (`fmtBytes(f.size)`: e.g. `2.4 MB`, `340 KB`).
895:      - A detected file type / MIME badge (e.g. `image/jpeg`).
896:      - A green `Ready to Upload` status indicator.
897:      - An immediate `✕` clear button (`clearFileSelection()`), allowing users to discard the file without reopening the operating system file picker.
898:   3. **Strict Industrial Aesthetics**: Styled with `border-radius: 0 !important;` and high-contrast dark tones matching the rest of the zero-trust industrial dashboard.
899:

259: ## 4. Accessing the Server from External Devices
260: 
261: You can connect external smartphones, tablets, and peer lab PCs to the simulated ESP32 without modifying any simulation files.
262: 
263: ### 4.1 Why Multi-Interface Access Works (0.0.0.0:9080 Binding)
264: When `wokwigw.exe` starts, it creates a socket listening on `0.0.0.0:9080` (`INADDR_ANY`). Rather than locking to loopback (`127.0.0.1`), it accepts incoming TCP packets on **every physical and virtual network adapter** active on the Windows host machine.
265: 
266: Any device that can ping or route to an IP address belonging to your host PC can access the ESP32 server over port `9080`.
267: 
268: ---
269: 
270: ### 4.2 Scenario 1: Home Hybrid Testing (Host on Wired Ethernet, Client Phone/Laptop on Router Wi-Fi)
271: In this home setup, your host workstation running the simulation is plugged into the Wi-Fi router via physical Ethernet cable, while your smartphone, tablet, or secondary laptop connects wirelessly to the same router:
272: 
273: ```
274:                       +------------------------------------------+
275:                       |         Home Wi-Fi Router Gateway        |
276:                       |          (Subnet: e.g. 192.168.0.1)      |
277:                       +--------------------+---------------------+
278:                                            |
279:                     +----------------------+----------------------+
280:                     | (Physical Ethernet)                         | (Wi-Fi 2.4/5 GHz)
281:                     ▼                                             ▼
282: +---------------------------------------+     +---------------------------------------+
283: |  Host PC (Running Simulation)         |     |  Mobile Device / Secondary Laptop     |
284: |  Ethernet IP: e.g., 192.168.0.105     |     |  Wi-Fi IP: e.g., 192.168.0.120        |
285: |  wokwigw.exe listening: 0.0.0.0:9080  |     |  Opens Browser to Host Ethernet IP:   |
286: |  setup_firewall.bat PORT 9080 ALLOWED |     |  http://192.168.0.105:9080/          |
287: +---------------------------------------+     +---------------------------------------+
288: ```
289: 
290: #### Step-by-Step Instructions:
291: 1. **Find the Host Ethernet IP**:
292:    - On the host PC running the simulation, open PowerShell and execute:
293:      ```powershell
294:      ipconfig
295:      ```
296:    - Locate the section titled **`Ethernet adapter Ethernet`** (or `Ethernet adapter vEthernet` / your main wired NIC).
297:    - Note the **`IPv4 Address`** (for example: `192.168.0.105` or `192.168.1.50`).
298:    > [!IMPORTANT]
299:    > Do **not** look for "Wireless LAN adapter Wi-Fi" on the host PC if it is plugged in via Ethernet! The host PC is communicating through its wired NIC, so client devices must target the host's **Ethernet IPv4 address**.
300: 
301: 2. **Verify Network Profile**:
302:    - Standard home routers bridge Ethernet LAN ports and Wi-Fi into the exact same broadcast subnet (`192.168.0.x`).
303:    - Run [`setup_firewall.bat`](setup_firewall.bat) as Administrator once to ensure inbound port 9080 is permitted.
304: 
305: 3. **Connect from Phone/Laptop**:
306:    - Ensure the phone or secondary laptop is connected to your home Wi-Fi SSID.
307:    - Open Chrome, Safari, or Firefox on the mobile device and navigate to:
308:      - **NAS File Dashboard**: `http://<HOST_ETHERNET_IP>:9080/` (e.g. `http://192.168.0.105:9080/`)
309:      - **Hosted Static Webpage**: `http://<HOST_ETHERNET_IP>:9080/site`
310: 
311: ---
312: 
313: ### 4.3 Scenario 2: Lab Workstation Testing (Both Devices on Wired Ethernet LAN Switch)
314: In the microprocessor laboratory, both the host workstation running the simulation (PC 1) and peer student workstations (PC 2) are connected via physical RJ45 Ethernet patch cables to the same campus lab switch:
315: 
316: ```
317:                       +------------------------------------------+
318:                       |         Campus Lab Ethernet Switch       |
319:                       |       (Local Subnet: e.g. 10.100.x.x)    |
320:                       +--------------------+---------------------+
```

390: ### 4.5 Scenario 4: All-Wireless Testing (Both Host Laptop/PC & Client Devices on Same Wi-Fi Network)
391: In typical student dorms, homes, or modern labs without physical Ethernet cabling, **both the host workstation (running the simulation) and the client devices (phones, tablets, secondary laptops) connect 100% wirelessly to the same Wi-Fi router / Access Point**:
392: 
393: ```
394:                       +------------------------------------------+
395:                       |         Local Wi-Fi Router / AP          |
396:                       |        (Local Subnet: e.g. 192.168.1.1)  |
397:                       +--------------------+---------------------+
398:                                            |
399:                     +----------------------+----------------------+
400:                     | (Wi-Fi 2.4/5 GHz)                           | (Wi-Fi 2.4/5 GHz)
401:                     ▼                                             ▼
402: +---------------------------------------+     +---------------------------------------+
403: |  Host PC (Running Simulation)         |     |  Mobile Device / Secondary Laptop     |
404: |  Wi-Fi IP: e.g., 192.168.1.150        |     |  Wi-Fi IP: e.g., 192.168.1.175        |
405: |  wokwigw.exe listening: 0.0.0.0:9080  |     |  Opens Browser to Host Wi-Fi IP:      |
406: |  setup_firewall.bat PORT 9080 ALLOWED |     |  http://192.168.1.150:9080/          |
407: +---------------------------------------+     +---------------------------------------+
408: ```
409: 
410: #### Step-by-Step Instructions:
411: 1. **Find the Host Wireless IP**:
412:    - On the host laptop or PC running VS Code, open PowerShell and run:
413:      ```powershell
414:      ipconfig
415:      ```
416:    - Look for the section titled **`Wireless LAN adapter Wi-Fi`** (or `Wi-Fi 2`).
417:    - Note the **`IPv4 Address`** (for example: `192.168.1.150` or `192.168.0.104`).
418:    > [!TIP]
419:    > Because the host is on Wi-Fi (no Ethernet cable plugged in), the active IP address listening on `0.0.0.0:9080` is your **Wireless LAN adapter IPv4 address**.
420: 
421: 2. **Verify Firewall & Router Isolation**:
422:    - Run [`setup_firewall.bat`](setup_firewall.bat) once with Admin privileges so Windows Firewall permits incoming TCP traffic on port 9080 from the local Wi-Fi subnet.
423:    - **Crucial Wi-Fi Router Nuance (AP / Client Isolation)**:
424:      - On standard home and personal Wi-Fi routers, wireless devices can freely talk to each other.
425:      - If you are on an institutional or enterprise campus Wi-Fi (which frequently enables "Client Isolation" or "Guest Mode" to block device-to-device traffic), the router will drop packets between two wireless devices. If connecting times out on campus Wi-Fi, simply switch to **Scenario 3 (Windows Mobile Hotspot)**.
426: 
427: 3. **Access Endpoints from Client Device**:
428:    - Ensure the mobile phone or secondary laptop is connected to the exact same Wi-Fi SSID.
429:    - Open any browser (Chrome, Safari, Edge, Firefox) on the client device and navigate to:
430:      - **NAS Dashboard**: `http://<HOST_WIFI_IP>:9080/` (e.g. `http://192.168.1.150:9080/`)
431:      - **Static Hosted Webpage**: `http://<HOST_WIFI_IP>:9080/site`
432:      - **REST File Telemetry API**: `http://<HOST_WIFI_IP>:9080/api/files`
433:

265: When `wokwigw.exe` starts, it creates a socket listening on `0.0.0.0:9080` (`INADDR_ANY`). Rather than locking to loopback (`127.0.0.1`), it accepts incoming TCP packets on **every physical and virtual network adapter** active on the Windows host machine.
266: 
267: Any device that can ping or route to an IP address belonging to your host PC can access the ESP32 server over port `9080`.
268: 
269: ---
270: 
271: ### 4.2 Scenario 1: Home Hybrid Testing (Host on Wired Ethernet, Client Phone/Laptop on Router Wi-Fi)
272: In this home setup, your host workstation running the simulation is plugged into the Wi-Fi router via physical Ethernet cable, while your smartphone, tablet, or secondary laptop connects wirelessly to the same router:
273: 
274: ```
275:                       +------------------------------------------+
276:                       |         Home Wi-Fi Router Gateway        |
277:                       |          (Subnet: e.g. 192.168.0.1)      |
278:                       +--------------------+---------------------+
279:                                            |
280:                     +----------------------+----------------------+
281:                     | (Physical Ethernet)                         | (Wi-Fi 2.4/5 GHz)
282:                     ▼                                             ▼
283: +---------------------------------------+     +---------------------------------------+
284: |  Host PC (Running Simulation)         |     |  Mobile Device / Secondary Laptop     |
285: |  Ethernet IP: e.g., 192.168.0.105     |     |  Wi-Fi IP: e.g., 192.168.0.120        |
286: |  wokwigw.exe listening: 0.0.0.0:9080  |     |  Opens Browser to Host Ethernet IP:   |
287: |  setup_firewall.bat PORT 9080 ALLOWED |     |  http://192.168.0.105:9080/          |
288: +---------------------------------------+     +---------------------------------------+
289: ```
290: 
291: #### Step-by-Step Instructions:
292: 1. **Find the Host Ethernet IP**:
293:    - On the host PC running the simulation, open PowerShell and execute:
294:      ```powershell
295:      ipconfig
296:      ```
297:    - Locate the section titled **`Ethernet adapter Ethernet`** (or `Ethernet adapter vEthernet` / your main wired NIC).
298:    - Note the **`IPv4 Address`** (for example: `192.168.0.105` or `192.168.1.50`).
299:    > [!IMPORTANT]
300:    > Do **not** look for "Wireless LAN adapter Wi-Fi" on the host PC if it is plugged in via Ethernet! The host PC is communicating through its wired NIC, so client devices must target the host's **Ethernet IPv4 address**.
301: 
302: 2. **Verify Network Profile**:
303:    - Standard home routers bridge Ethernet LAN ports and Wi-Fi into the exact same broadcast subnet (`192.168.0.x`).
304:    - Run [`setup_firewall.bat`](setup_firewall.bat) as Administrator once to ensure inbound port 9080 is permitted.
305: 
306: 3. **Connect from Phone/Laptop**:
307:    - Ensure the phone or secondary laptop is connected to your home Wi-Fi SSID.
308:    - Open Chrome, Safari, or Firefox on the mobile device and navigate to:
309:      - **NAS File Dashboard**: `http://<HOST_ETHERNET_IP>:9080/` (e.g. `http://192.168.0.105:9080/`)
310:      - **Hosted Static Webpage**: `http://<HOST_ETHERNET_IP>:9080/site`
311:

315: In the microprocessor laboratory, both the host workstation running the simulation (PC 1) and peer student workstations (PC 2) are connected via physical RJ45 Ethernet patch cables to the same campus lab switch:
316: 
317: ```
318:                       +------------------------------------------+
319:                       |         Campus Lab Ethernet Switch       |
320:                       |       (Local Subnet: e.g. 10.100.x.x)    |
321:                       +--------------------+---------------------+
322:                                            |
323:                     +----------------------+----------------------+
324:                     | (Ethernet Cable 1)                          | (Ethernet Cable 2)
325:                     ▼                                             ▼
```

408: +---------------------------------------+     +---------------------------------------+

411: #### Step-by-Step Instructions:
412: 1. **Find the Host Wireless IP**:

414:      ```powershell

416:      ```

418:    - Note the **`IPv4 Address`** (for example: `192.168.1.150` or `192.168.0.104`).
419:    > [!TIP]
420:    > Because the host is on Wi-Fi (no Ethernet cable plugged in), the active IP address listening on `0.0.0.0:9080` is your **Wireless LAN adapter IPv4 address**.
421: 
422: 2. **Verify Firewall & Router Isolation**:
423:    - Run [`setup_firewall.bat`](setup_firewall.bat) once with Admin privileges so Windows Firewall permits incoming TCP traffic on port 9080 from the local Wi-Fi subnet.
424:    - **Crucial Wi-Fi Router Nuance (AP / Client Isolation)**:
425:      - On standard home and personal Wi-Fi routers, wireless devices can freely talk to each other.
426:      - If you are on an institutional or enterprise campus Wi-Fi (which frequently enables "Client Isolation" or "Guest Mode" to block device-to-device traffic), the router will drop packets between two wireless devices. If connecting times out on campus Wi-Fi, simply switch to **Scenario 3 (Windows Mobile Hotspot)**.

394: During project defense or when network access in the lab is restricted (e.g. campus Wi-Fi has strict Client/AP Isolation blocking inter-device communication), turn your host laptop into a Wi-Fi Access Point using Windows Mobile Hotspot:
395:

399: |  1. Enable Windows Mobile Hotspot (Share over: Wi-Fi)                             |
400: |  2. Windows automatically assigns Host Gateway IP: 192.168.137.1                  |
401: |  3. wokwigw.exe listens on 0.0.0.0:9080 (Binds directly to virtual hotspot NIC)  |

418:    - Note the **Network name (SSID)** and **Password**.

420:    - Windows automatically assigns the host PC the virtual IP **`192.168.137.1`** on the Microsoft Wi-Fi Direct Virtual Adapter.
421:    - This IP is **always identical** across all Windows machines, making it completely predictable for live presentations.
422: 3. **Connect Client Mobile Devices**:
423:    - On evaluators' or team members' phones/tablets, connect to the laptop hotspot SSID.

426:      - **NAS Dashboard**: `http://192.168.137.1:9080/`
427:      - **Static Site**: `http://192.168.137.1:9080/site`

453: #### Step-by-Step Instructions:
454: 1. **Find the Host Wireless IP**:
455:    - On the host laptop or PC running VS Code, open PowerShell and run:
456:      ```powershell
457:      ipconfig

460:    - Note the **`IPv4 Address`** (for example: `192.168.1.150` or `192.168.0.104`).
461:    > [!TIP]
462:    > Because the host is on Wi-Fi (no Ethernet cable plugged in), the active IP address listening on `0.0.0.0:9080` is your **Wireless LAN adapter IPv4 address**.
463: 
464: 2. **Verify Firewall & Router Isolation**:
465:    - Run [`setup_firewall.bat`](setup_firewall.bat) once with Admin privileges so Windows Firewall permits incoming TCP traffic on port 9080 from the local Wi-Fi subnet.
466:    - **Crucial Wi-Fi Router Nuance (AP / Client Isolation)**:
467:      - On standard home and personal Wi-Fi routers, wireless devices can freely talk to each other.
468:      - If you are on an institutional or enterprise campus Wi-Fi (which frequently enables "Client Isolation" or "Guest Mode" to block device-to-device traffic), the router will drop packets between two wireless devices. If connecting times out on campus Wi-Fi, simply switch to **Scenario 3 (Windows Mobile Hotspot)**.
469: 
470: 3. **Access Endpoints from Client Device**:
471:    - Ensure the mobile phone or secondary laptop is connected to the exact same Wi-Fi SSID.
472:    - Open any browser (Chrome, Safari, Edge, Firefox) on the client device and navigate to:
473:      - **NAS Dashboard**: `http://<HOST_WIFI_IP>:9080/` (e.g. `http://192.168.1.150:9080/`)
474:      - **Static Hosted Webpage**: `http://<HOST_WIFI_IP>:9080/site`
475:      - **REST File Telemetry API**: `http://<HOST_WIFI_IP>:9080/api/files`

511: ## 5. Zero-Install Local Network File Sharing (LocalSend Web Model)
512: 
513: ### 5.1 Bi-Directional File Transfer Workflow
514: `Project.MM` functions identically to the popular **LocalSend "Share via Browser"** web feature. No software or apps need to be installed on client devices:
515: 
516: ```text
517:   [Lab PC 1: Host Node]                                 [Lab PC 2: Peer Client]
518:   +----------------------------------+                  +----------------------------------+
519:   | Wokwi Simulator (ESP32 DevKit)   |                  | Standard Web Browser             |
520:   |   ↕ (ws://localhost:9011)        |                  | (Chrome / Edge / Safari)         |
521:   | wokwigw.exe (0.0.0.0:9080)       |                  |                                  |
522:   | Windows Firewall Port 9080 OPEN  |                  | Navigates to:                    |
523:   +-----------------+----------------+                  | http://<HOST_IP>:9080/           |
524:                     |                                   +-----------------+----------------+
525:                     |                                                     |
```

545: #### 1. Why Multi-Interface Routing Works (`0.0.0.0:9080` Binding)
546: - The network bridge `wokwigw.exe` binds by default to socket address `0.0.0.0:9080` (`INADDR_ANY`), not just loopback `127.0.0.1`.
547: - This means it listens on **all active network interfaces** on your Windows host machine at the same time.
548: - **Firewall Rule Automation**: Windows Firewall blocks unprompted inbound connections by default. Running [`setup_firewall.bat`](https://github.com/b1tranger/Microprocessor_Assembly_Lab/blob/main/Project.MM/LocalConfig/setup_firewall.bat) automatically requests UAC elevation and opens TCP port 9080 across all profiles via:
549:   ```powershell
550:   New-NetFirewallRule -DisplayName "Wokwi Gateway NAS" -Direction Inbound -LocalPort 9080 -Protocol TCP -Profile Any -Action Allow
551:   ```
552: 
553: #### 2. Multi-Interface Deployment Configurations:
554: * **Method A (Windows Mobile Hotspot)**: Turn on **Windows Mobile Hotspot** (Settings > Network & internet > Mobile hotspot). Windows assigns the host PC virtual gateway IP **`192.168.137.1`**. Evaluators connect their smartphones/tablets to this hotspot and open `http://192.168.137.1:9080/`. No campus router or external Wi-Fi login is required!
555: * **Method B (Shared Local Wi-Fi Router — All-Wireless, No Ethernet)**: When both the host laptop and client devices (smartphones, tablets, peer laptops) connect wirelessly to the same home, lab, or office Wi-Fi router (e.g. `192.168.1.x`). Run `ipconfig` on the host to obtain the **`Wireless LAN adapter Wi-Fi`** IPv4 address (e.g. `192.168.1.150`). Client devices open `http://<HOST_WIFI_IP>:9080/`. *(Note: Requires router AP/Client Isolation to be disabled)*.
556: * **Method C (Wired Ethernet LAN Switch)**: Plug into the lab Ethernet switch. Find your host IP via `ipconfig` under Ethernet adapter (e.g., `192.168.0.105` or `10.100.x.x`). Any lab desktop PC on the wired switch navigates to `http://<YOUR_LAN_IP>:9080/`.
557:

567: - **Internal Web Server**: The HTTP server is **100% native to the ESP32 C++ firmware** (`WebServer server(80)`). There is **no Apache or Nginx** running on the PC; the microcontroller itself handles socket creation, routing, and FAT32 streaming.
568: 
569: #### 7.3.1 LocalSend Web Model: 2-Computer Lab File Sharing
570: In popular file-transfer tools like **LocalSend**, the **"Share via Browser" (LocalSend Web)** feature enables zero-installation file sharing: one computer starts a temporary web server on the local network, and any other device on the LAN navigates to that IP in a browser to upload or download files without installing an app.
571: 
572: `Project.MM` reproduces this exact user-friendly workflow for laboratory evaluations, but with key **microprocessor architecture advantages**:
573: 1. **Zero Client Setup**: Neither Computer 1 nor Computer 2 needs specialized software installed. A standard browser (Chrome, Edge, Firefox) is all that is required.
574: 2. **True Embedded Hardware Node**: Unlike LocalSend Web (which is a heavy software desktop program running on an OS with 16 GB RAM and storing files on an internal PC SSD), `Project.MM` executes on an **ESP32 microcontroller** interfacing a **FAT32 MicroSD card over the hardware VSPI bus**.
575: 3. **Decoupled Standalone Appliance**: Both computers are equal clients to the ESP32 storage pool. File exchanges do not depend on the sender's desktop OS remaining awake.

771: 
772: ### Q5: How does the web server avoid blocking other background tasks?
773: - **Rebuttal**: We take advantage of the ESP32's dual-core Xtensa architecture and the FreeRTOS real-time operating system. Time-critical background operations (like sensor telemetry or network health tests) are pinned to Core 1 using `xTaskCreatePinnedToCore`, while the networking stack runs independently on Core 0.
774: 
775: ---
776: 
777: ### Q6: Does the file server only work on localhost, or can other network devices connect?
778: - **Rebuttal**: It is fully accessible across the entire local network through three distinct deployment topologies:
779:   1. **Deterministic Hotspot**: Enabling Windows Mobile Hotspot assigns the host PC `192.168.137.1`. Any smartphone or laptop connecting to the hotspot accesses `http://192.168.137.1:9080/` with zero router dependencies.
780:   2. **Shared Wireless Wi-Fi (All-Wireless)**: Both the host PC and external mobile devices connect wirelessly to the same Wi-Fi router. Clients navigate to `http://<HOST_WIFI_IP>:9080/` without any physical cables.
781:   3. **Wired Campus LAN Switch**: Lab PCs on the same Ethernet switch access the server at `http://<HOST_ETHERNET_IP>:9080/`.
782:   4. **Physical Silicon**: On real hardware, the ESP32 either connects to the local router or broadcasts its own autonomous SoftAP (`192.168.4.1`), serving all network clients on standard port 80 with no host computer required.
783: 
784: ---
785: 
786: ### Q7: Why did Wokwi Cloud show a paywall, and how does your project bypass it?
787: - **Rebuttal**: Wokwi Cloud's free tier provides a Public Gateway that only supports outbound NAT requests (e.g. hitting weather APIs), but blocks inbound TCP connections from external desktop browsers unless subscribing to their paid Private Gateway ($7–$15/mo). We bypassed this in two ways:
788:   1. For cloud users, [`Project.MM/CloudConfig`](https://github.com/b1tranger/Microprocessor_Assembly_Lab/blob/main/Project.MM/CloudConfig) uses an internal FreeRTOS loopback client (`runClientTests` on `127.0.0.1`) that tests all endpoints 100% for free inside the simulator.
789:   2. For full interactive browser testing, [`Project.MM/LocalConfig`](https://github.com/b1tranger/Microprocessor_Assembly_Lab/blob/main/Project.MM/LocalConfig) runs locally in VS Code with the free community license and local `wokwigw.exe` bridge.
790: 
791: ---
792: 
793: ### Q8: Why choose Classic ESP32 with SPI over an ESP32-S3 with a USB flash drive?
794: - **Rebuttal**: The Classic ESP32 (WROOM-32) with a SPI MicroSD module costs under 400 BDT, is ubiquitously available, has a mature, rock-solid Arduino `SD` library, and aligns 100% with the pinout table submitted in our course proposal (`GPIO 5, 18, 19, 23`). While the ESP32-S3 supports native USB host for pen drives, it requires complex USB MSC drivers and different pin configurations.
795: 
796: ---
797: 
798: ### Q9: How would this system operate in a field environment without an internet router?
799: - **Rebuttal**: The ESP32 natively supports **Soft Access Point (SoftAP) Mode** (`WiFi.softAP()`). In an off-grid forest or disaster zone, the ESP32 broadcasts its own Wi-Fi SSID (`"ESP32-Edge-NAS"`). Field personnel connect their smartphones directly to the ESP32 and access files at `http://192.168.4.1/` without needing an internet connection, external router, or PC.
800: 
801: ---
802: 
803: ### Q10: How does this system compare to LocalSend / LocalSend Web?
804: - **Rebuttal**: LocalSend's "Share via Browser" (Web Share) mode turns a desktop PC into a temporary web server on the local network so other machines can transfer files in a browser without installing the app. Our project provides that exact same zero-install browser experience for lab computers. However, from an embedded systems perspective, `Project.MM` is fundamentally distinct: it runs on a \$4 ESP32 microcontroller with 520 KB SRAM rather than a multi-gigabyte PC OS, writes files across hardware VSPI lines directly into FAT32 MicroSD card sectors with a strict ~2 KB RAM streaming overhead, and acts as an autonomous hardware appliance that does not depend on a host PC remaining online.
805: 
806: ---
807: 
808: ### Q11: How do you handle campus Wi-Fi AP/Client Isolation during a lab demonstration?
809: - **Rebuttal**: University routers and enterprise switches often enforce AP/Client Isolation to prevent peer-to-peer communication between connected devices. To guarantee that our live demonstration is never blocked by institutional firewall policies, we activate **Windows Mobile Hotspot** on the host workstation. Windows configures a virtual NAT gateway at `192.168.137.1`. Any smartphone or lab computer connecting to this hotspot can reach `http://192.168.137.1:9080/` with zero router restrictions.
810: 
811: ---
812: 
813: ### Q12: Why is the dashboard styled with sharp geometry (border-radius: 0) and no animated status dot?
814: - **Rebuttal**: In professional high-density engineering appliances and telemetry consoles, curved borders introduce unnecessary visual noise and table misalignment. By establishing a strict `border-radius: 0 !important;` rule and removing distracting pulsating online badges, the interface emphasizes immediate data density, high-contrast monospace technical readability, and modern matte aesthetics.
815: 
816: ---
817: 
818: ### Q13: Why did uploads stay stuck at 100% for several seconds before completing?
819: - **Rebuttal**: In our simulation architecture, client uploads traverse the host machine's loopback interface at gigabit speed, filling the OS socket buffer almost immediately so `xhr.upload.onprogress` reaches 100% in milliseconds. However, the virtual ESP32 runs at cycle-accurate simulation speed, bit-banging and clocking each 512-byte sector across the simulated VSPI bus into the virtual FAT32 SD card. In the web UI, we introduced a dedicated commit transition state (`Writing to Storage`, `⚡ Committing...`, `⏱ Finalizing SD card write`) to explicitly inform users that network delivery has finished and the simulated microcontroller is actively committing blocks to storage.
820: 
821: ---
822: 
823: ### Q14: How does your firmware guarantee zero corrupted or 0-byte files if an upload is interrupted?
824: - **Rebuttal**: In `handleFileUpload()`, on `UPLOAD_FILE_ABORTED` or on write error detection, the firmware immediately closes the active file handle and invokes `SD.remove(currentUploadTarget)`. Furthermore, the POST completion callback strictly verifies `upload.status == UPLOAD_FILE_END && upload.totalSize > 0 && !uploadWriteError`; otherwise, it returns HTTP 500 JSON error. This ensures aborted uploads never linger as empty 0-byte entries on FAT32.
825:

73: ## 3. Analysis & Key Insights (Root Cause Investigation)
74: 
75: ### 3.1 The Failure Signature (`0 / 4096 bytes written`)
76: In `src/main.cpp#L347-L377`, the upload lifecycle proceeds as:
77: 1. `UPLOAD_FILE_START`: `SD.mkdir("/uploads")` and `SD.open("/uploads/IMG-20261113-WA0003.jpeg", FILE_WRITE)` execute. Because `uploadFile` evaluates to true, the file handle opens successfully and prints:
78:    `[UPLOAD START] Destination: /uploads/IMG-20261113-WA0003.jpeg`.
79: 2. `UPLOAD_FILE_WRITE`: Incoming TCP segments from the foreign device (typically 1,436-byte segments) fill the intermediate RAM buffer `uploadWriteBuffer`.
80: 3. When `uploadWriteBufferIndex == 4096`, the firmware calls:
81:    `size_t written = uploadFile.write(uploadWriteBuffer, 4096);`
82: 4. The return value `written` was **`0`**, immediately triggering:
83:    `[UPLOAD ERROR] Sector write failed: 0 / 4096 bytes written. Aborting.`
84: 
85: ### 3.2 Hardware Sector Architecture & The Multi-Sector Pitfall
86: In physical SD cards and the FAT32 filesystem:
87: - The fundamental physical sector size is strictly **512 bytes** (`GET_SECTOR_SIZE: 512`).
88: - A 4,096-byte write represents exactly **8 contiguous sectors** ($8 \times 512 = 4096$).
89: - When FatFs receives a write request that is a clean multiple of the physical sector size, its internal optimization attempts a direct multi-block write (`disk_write(..., count = 8)`).
90: 
91: ### 3.3 FatFs & `sd_diskio.cpp` Execution Flow
92: Tracing into the ESP-IDF SD driver ([`sd_diskio.cpp#L688-L707`](https://github.com/b1tranger/Microprocessor_Assembly_Lab/blob/main/Project.MM/setup/PlatformIO_Espressif_Offline_Installer/.platformio/packages/framework-arduinoespressif32/libraries/SD/src/sd_diskio.cpp#L688-L707)):
93: 
94: ```cpp
95: if (count > 1) {
96:   res = sdWriteSectors(pdrv, (const char *)buffer, sector, count) ? RES_OK : RES_ERROR;
97: } else {
98:   res = sdWriteSector(pdrv, (const char *)buffer, sector) ? RES_OK : RES_ERROR;
99: }
100: ```
101: 
102: When `count > 1` (here `count = 8`):
103: 1. `sdWriteSectors` is invoked.
104: 2. In `sdWriteSectors#L346-L350`, the driver attempts to pre-erase the 8 sectors before writing by issuing **`ACMD23` (`SET_WR_BLK_ERASE_COUNT`)**:
105:    ```cpp
106:    if (card->type != CARD_MMC) {
107:      if (sdTransaction(pdrv, SET_WR_BLK_ERASE_COUNT, currentCount, NULL)) {
108:        return false; // Immediately aborts before writing anything!
109:      }
110:    }
111:    ```
112: 3. `SET_WR_BLK_ERASE_COUNT` is an optional Application-Specific Command (`CMD55` followed by `CMD23`).
113: 4. **Wokwi's virtual SD component (`wokwi-microsd-card`) and many physical SPI-mode micro-SD modules do not support `ACMD23` or `CMD25` multi-block write in SPI mode!**
114: 5. The SD controller responds with an error token (`0x04` Illegal Command), causing `sdTransaction` to return failure.
115: 6. `sdWriteSectors` immediately returns `false` without writing a single byte.
116: 7. `fwrite` receives `RES_ERROR` and returns **`0` bytes written**.
117: 
118: ### 3.4 Why Single-Sector 512-Byte Writes (`CMD24`) Succeed Universally
119: When `UPLOAD_SECTOR_BUFFER_SIZE` is configured to **512 bytes**:
120: 1. Every write to `uploadFile.write()` is passed as `512` bytes.
121: 2. FatFs dispatches `disk_write(..., count = 1)`.
122: 3. Because `count == 1`, the driver dispatches `sdWriteSector` instead of `sdWriteSectors`.
123: 4. `sdWriteSector` sends **`CMD24` (`WRITE_BLOCK_SINGLE`)** with start token `0xFE`.
124: 5. `CMD24` never issues `ACMD23` or `CMD25`. It is 100% universally supported across all SD cards, micro-SD cards, SPI modes, Wokwi virtual media, and physical ESP32 breadboard circuits.
125: 
126: ### 3.5 Hardening Fallback Seeding Writes
127: In `phase1_seedInitialFiles()`, `handleRoot()`, and `handleSite()`, large asset buffers (such as `fileserver.html` at 23,138 bytes) were previously written with a single call `f.write(data, size)`. These routines were refactored to stream data in $\le 512$-byte slices, guaranteeing single-sector `CMD24` operations throughout the entire codebase.
128: 
129: ---
130: 
131: ## 4. Final Solution & Outcomes (Firmware Hardening)
132: - Refactored `Project.MM/LocalConfig/src/main.cpp`:
133:   ```cpp
134:   // 512-Byte Sector-Aligned FAT32 SD Write Buffer
135:   // Physical SD block size is 512 bytes. Flushes of exactly 512 bytes force
136:   // sd_diskio to invoke CMD24 (WRITE_BLOCK_SINGLE). Blocks >512 bytes trigger
137:   // multi-sector CMD25 + ACMD23 (SET_WR_BLK_ERASE_COUNT), which Wokwi and SPI adapters reject.
138:   #define UPLOAD_SECTOR_BUFFER_SIZE 512
139:   static uint8_t uploadWriteBuffer[UPLOAD_SECTOR_BUFFER_SIZE];
140:   ```
141: - Guaranteed zero aborted uploads when receiving data from mobile devices or external PCs.
142:

166: ### 5.2 Host Wi-Fi IP Resolution & Subnet Traversal
167: 1. On the host laptop, run `ipconfig`.
168: 2. Locate **`Wireless LAN adapter Wi-Fi`** and read the `IPv4 Address` (e.g. `192.168.1.150`).
169: 3. Client mobile phones connected to the same Wi-Fi SSID navigate directly to:
170:    - `http://<HOST_WIFI_IP>:9080/` (Dashboard)
171:    - `http://<HOST_WIFI_IP>:9080/site` (Hosted static website)
172: 
173: ### 5.3 Enterprise AP / Client Isolation Nuance
174: Public campus Wi-Fi networks frequently enforce **AP / Client Isolation**, which drops peer-to-peer packets between wireless clients. If an all-wireless connection times out on university Wi-Fi:
175: - Fall back to **Scenario 3 (Windows Mobile Hotspot)**, where the host laptop acts as the private DHCP gateway (`192.168.137.1`), bypassing campus infrastructure entirely.
176:

179: ## 6. Mobile File Selection Details Preview Card
180: 
181: ### 6.1 The Mobile UX Problem
182: On mobile browsers (Chrome / Safari on Android and iOS), the native `<input type="file">` selector renders a full-width system button (`Choose file`). Because of restricted screen width and default browser styling:
183: - Selected file names were pushed below or truncated into ellipses (`IMG-202...`).
184: - Users received zero visual feedback regarding file size, file format, or whether the file was ready to upload before tapping the submission button.
185: 
186: ### 6.2 Frontend Architecture (`.file-detail-card`)
187: Implemented a high-contrast, minimalist dark detail card in [`data/www/fileserver.html`](https://github.com/b1tranger/Microprocessor_Assembly_Lab/blob/main/Project.MM/LocalConfig/data/www/fileserver.html):
188: ```html
189: <div id="fileDetailCard" class="file-detail-card" style="display: none;">
190:   <div class="file-detail-main">
191:     <span class="file-detail-icon">📄</span>
192:     <div class="file-detail-meta">
193:       <div class="file-detail-name" id="chosenFileName">No file selected</div>
194:       <div class="file-detail-tags">
195:         <span class="file-detail-badge" id="chosenFileSize">0 B</span>
196:         <span class="file-detail-badge" id="chosenFileType">Unknown</span>
197:         <span class="file-detail-status">Ready to Upload</span>
198:       </div>
199:     </div>
200:   </div>
201:   <button type="button" class="btn-clear-file" id="clearFileBtn" title="Clear selection" onclick="clearFileSelection();">✕</button>
202: </div>
203: ```
204: 
205: ### 6.3 Telemetry Display & Reset Lifecycle
206: - **Dynamic Event Listener**: Listens to `change` on `fileSelect`. Extracts `f.name`, formatted size via `fmtBytes(f.size)`, and detected MIME type/extension.
207: - **Instant Clear (`clearFileSelection()`)**: Tapping the `✕` button immediately empties the input value and hides the preview card.
208: - **Upload Lifecycle**: Automatically clears after upload completion (`xhr.onload`).
209: 
210: ---
211: 
212: ## 7. Evaluator Q&A Defense Expansion (Q2, Q6, Q17 – Q22)
213: 
214: ### 7.1 Core Revisions in Existing Questions (Q2 & Q6)
215: - **Q2 (Memory Footprint)**: Updated rebuttal from 4KB buffering to **512-byte single-sector alignment**, strictly capping RAM consumption to ~2 KB and documenting single-sector `CMD24` (`WRITE_BLOCK_SINGLE`) execution.
216: - **Q6 (Multi-Device Topologies)**: Expanded from dual methods to **Tri-Deployment Configurations** detailing:
217:   1. Deterministic Gateway Hotspot (`192.168.137.1`).
218:   2. Shared Wireless Wi-Fi Router (`<HOST_WIFI_IP>:9080`, with both host and client devices 100% wireless).
219:   3. Campus Wired Ethernet Switch (`<HOST_ETHERNET_IP>:9080`).
220: 
221: ### 7.2 Q17: Why HTTP and Not HTTPS (TLS/SSL)?
222: - **RAM Overhead of TLS**: Establishing a single TLS 1.2/1.3 session via `mbedTLS` on ESP32 consumes **45 KB to 65 KB of internal SRAM** for asymmetric cipher state machines, session keys, and certificate chain buffers. On an ESP32 with ~320 KB accessible user heap, handling multiple concurrent HTTPS connections quickly causes heap fragmentation and socket starvation (`ENOMEM`).
223: - **Cryptographic Computation Bottleneck**: Microcontroller CPUs lack dedicated hardware acceleration for high-entropy asymmetric public-key handshakes (RSA 2048/4096 or ECDSA), introducing multi-second connection latencies and dropping streaming transfer throughput below 150 KB/s.
224: - **Air-Gapped & Local LAN Boundary**: `Project.MM` is designed as an air-gapped edge appliance for isolated subnets, emergency off-grid nodes, and local Wi-Fi networks protected by physical layer security (WPA2/WPA3 enterprise Wi-Fi or direct peer-to-peer SoftAP). Traffic never crosses public internet routing hops.
225: - **Self-Signed Certificate Friction**: In local IP deployments (`192.168.x.x`), HTTPS requires self-signed certificates, which cause modern smartphone and desktop browsers to throw intrusive security warning interstitials ("Your connection is not private") that disrupt zero-install field access.
226: - **Enterprise Architecture Pattern**: In production deployments requiring WAN access, embedded engineers place the ESP32 behind an edge reverse proxy (such as Nginx, Caddy, or Cloudflare Tunnel) on the router or gateway. The proxy handles public TLS termination, while the ESP32 remains lean, ultra-responsive, and dedicated to raw SPI/FAT32 I/O.
227: 
228: ### 7.3 Q18: Why Max 256 MB in Simulation vs Physical Reality?
229: - **Wokwi Simulation Engine Limit**: In Wokwi for VS Code and Wokwi CLI, **`256M` is the hardcoded upper capacity limit** for the virtual `wokwi-microsd-card` component (the default is 8 MB, and the maximum configurable value in `wokwi.toml` is 256 MB). Attempting values like `512M` or `1G` throws a simulator validation error.
230: - **Host Startup & Writeback Performance**: In simulation, Wokwi formats the virtual disk into host RAM upon boot and writes modified sectors back to `data/network/` on your SSD when stopped. Keeping the virtual disk at 256 MB guarantees near-instant simulation boot times (< 2 seconds) and rapid file synchronization.
231: - **Zero Limit on Physical Silicon**: **This limit does NOT exist on physical hardware.** The ESP32 Arduino FAT32 driver (`SD.h` / FatFs) standardly supports physical SDHC MicroSD cards up to **32 GB** (and exFAT/FAT32 formatted cards up to **128 GB - 2 TB** with standard 32 KB cluster allocation).
232: 
233: ### 7.4 Q19: Real-World Hardware Configurations (Minimum vs Maximum)
234: - **Bare Minimum Real-World Hardware & Firmware Configuration (Ultra-Low Cost & Field Battery Node)**:
235:   - **Microcontroller**: Classic ESP32-WROOM-32 (240 MHz dual-core Xtensa LX6, 520 KB internal SRAM, 4 MB external SPI Flash). Under-clockable to **80 MHz or 160 MHz** via `setCpuFrequencyMhz()` to drop power consumption to < 35 mA.
236:   - **RAM Footprint**: Static firmware allocation ~38 KB; fixed **~2 KB streaming memory window** using our 512-byte sector-aligned buffer for file transfers.
237:   - **Physical Storage**: Standard 1 GB to 4 GB Class 4/10 MicroSD card formatted with FAT32 (512-byte physical sectors).
238:   - **Hardware Interface**: Hardware VSPI (`GPIO 18` SCK, `GPIO 19` MISO, `GPIO 23` MOSI, `GPIO 5` CS) with standard 10k pull-up resistors on MISO/MOSI, clocked at 4 MHz to 10 MHz.
239:   - **Power Supply**: Single 3.7V 18650 Lithium-ion cell (2600 mAh) paired with a TP4056 charge controller and a low-dropout 3.3V regulator (e.g. ME6211 or AMS1117-3.3 capable of 500 mA peak Wi-Fi TX bursts).
240:   - **Network**: Autonomous SoftAP mode (`WiFi.softAP("ESP32-Edge-NAS")`) serving clients at default gateway `http://192.168.4.1/` with zero router or internet connection required.
241: - **Maximum / High-Performance Real-World Configuration (Enterprise Industrial Edge NAS)**:
242:   - **Microcontroller**: ESP32-S3-WROOM-2 or ESP32-WROVER-E with **8 MB to 16 MB Octal PSRAM** and **16 MB to 32 MB Quad/Octal SPI Flash** running at full 240 MHz.
243:   - **Physical Storage**: High-endurance 32 GB to 64 GB SanDisk/Samsung Extreme UHS-I MicroSD card.
244:   - **Hardware Interface**: **4-bit SDMMC Hardware Mode** (`SD_MMC.h` utilizing 4 data lines: `D0-D3`, `CLK`, `CMD`), clocked at **40 MHz to 50 MHz**. This increases real-world read/write bandwidth from ~1.2 MB/s (SPI) to **10 MB/s - 15 MB/s**. Alternatively, on the ESP32-S3, native USB 2.0 OTG Host mode (`USBHost.h`) can mount external USB thumb drives or external SSDs directly.
245:   - **Concurrency & OS**: FreeRTOS multi-core pinned tasks: Core 0 handles lwIP network protocol processing and high-throughput TCP windowing; Core 1 handles asynchronous non-blocking WebServer routes, multipart FAT32 chunking, and WebSocket telemetry push.
246:   - **Power Optimization**: Dynamic Frequency Scaling (DFS) with automatic modem sleep when idle, and deep-sleep current draw under **15 $\mu$A** during inactivity, waking up via capacitive touch or PIR motion sensor.
247: 
248: ### 7.5 Q20: Driver Rejection Mechanics (ACMD23/CMD25 vs CMD24)
249: - **Problem**: 4KB buffering triggered `sdWriteSectors(count = 8)`. Under the hood, this attempts to issue `ACMD23` (`SET_WR_BLK_ERASE_COUNT`), which Wokwi and cheap SPI boards reject with `0x04` Illegal Command, causing `0 / 4096 bytes written`.
250: - **Solution**: Setting `UPLOAD_SECTOR_BUFFER_SIZE 512` forces `count == 1`. This routes execution strictly to `sdWriteSector()`, issuing `CMD24` (`WRITE_BLOCK_SINGLE`) with token `0xFE`, which has 100% universal support.
251: 
252: ### 7.6 Q21: Concurrency, FreeRTOS Tasks & Socket Hygiene
253: - Dual-core task distribution ensures Core 0 handles lwIP while Core 1 handles HTTP.
254: - Background self-tests (`runClientTests`) drain response streams completely (`stream->read()`) and yield cooperatively (`vTaskDelay(800)`), preventing socket starvation.
255: - Aborted uploads immediately close handles and remove incomplete files via `SD.remove()`.
256: 
257: ### 7.7 Q22: Mobile Responsive File Details Preview Architecture
258: - Solves native mobile file input text clipping and truncation on narrow screens.
259: - Displays immediate monospace card showing chosen filename, exact formatted size (`fmtBytes`), detected MIME/extension badge, ready-to-upload indicator, and quick `✕` clear button.
```

#### Content
### Why Scenario 1 and Scenario 4 Appeared Identical on the Surface

In both scenarios, an external mobile device or secondary laptop accesses the ESP32 file server by navigating to `http://<HOST_IP>:9080/`. To a student or evaluator quickly skimming the steps:
1. Run `ipconfig`
2. Find an IPv4 address
3. Type `http://<IP>:9080/` into a smartphone browser

Because the high-level workflow ends in the same action, they appeared redundant.

---

### The 4 Critical Architectural & Operational Divergences

Under the hood, **Scenario 1** and **Scenario 4** address two physically and logically distinct environments:

| Engineering Dimension | Scenario 1: Home Hybrid LAN | Scenario 4: All-Wireless LAN |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Host Workstation Setup** | **Desktop PC / Docked Laptop** physically connected to the router via **RJ-45 Ethernet cable**. | **Laptop / Mobile PC** running on **100% Wi-Fi (No Ethernet cables connected)**. |
| **Client Device Setup** | Smartphone, tablet, or laptop on Router Wi-Fi. | Smartphone, tablet, or laptop on the exact same Wi-Fi SSID. |
| **Adapter to Select in `ipconfig`** | **`Ethernet adapter Ethernet`** (e.g. `192.168.0.105`). Wi-Fi is often disconnected or absent. | **`Wireless LAN adapter Wi-Fi`** (e.g. `192.168.1.150`). Ethernet shows **`Media disconnected`**. |
| **Common User Trap** | If a desktop user looks for "Wi-Fi" in `ipconfig`, they find nothing or select an inactive virtual NIC. | If a laptop user looks for "Ethernet", they see `Media disconnected` and assume networking is broken. |
| **Physical Packet Path** | Phone $\rightarrow$ Wi-Fi Radio $\rightarrow$ **Router Switch ASIC** $\rightarrow$ Host Ethernet Port. | Phone $\rightarrow$ Wi-Fi Radio $\rightarrow$ **Access Point BSSID** $\rightarrow$ Host Wi-Fi Radio. |
| **Campus AP Isolation Risk** | **Immune**: Routers bridge wired Ethernet ports directly to the LAN broadcast domain. | **High Risk**: University campus / dorm Wi-Fi enforces **Client Isolation** (drops peer station frames). |
| **Failure Mode** | Almost never fails on personal or lab networks. | Fails with **`ERR_CONNECTION_TIMED_OUT`** on university/public Wi-Fi. |
| **Immediate Failover** | N/A | **Switch immediately to [Scenario 3 (Windows Hotspot)](#45-scenario-3-portable-showcase-hotspot-host-laptop-hotspot-with-mobile-clients)**. |

---

`sdDeselectCard(pdrv)` is called *before* checking the status of the write operation. This means the SD card is deselected *while* it's busy writing, potentially causing the `SEND_STATUS` command to fail. `sdTransaction` relies on the card being selected. The critical flaw is deselecting the card prematurely. The design needs to be revised to ensure the card is selected until the write is complete, and the status can be confirmed.
```

```text
The `loop()` function calls `server.handleClient()`, which seems to manage client uploads. The first upload of `test1.txt` succeeded, writing 20 bytes. The second upload, `Screenshot_20261114-111618_Chrome.jpg`, failed, with a "Sector write failed" error, indicating a problem writing to the destination.


The successful write of `test1.txt` (20 bytes) contrasts with the failed write of the larger `Screenshot_20261114-111618_Chrome.jpg`. The key difference is the size of the data written in a single call. FatFs seems to buffer writes smaller than 512 bytes, only flushing to disk during `f_close` or `f_sync`. It's likely the failure occurs when a 512-byte write is attempted directly.


The `uploadFile.write(buf, 512)` function likely doesn't directly call the low-level disk write; instead, it writes to a buffered stream due to `setvbuf()`. This explains why the initial smaller file write (20 bytes) succeeded because the buffer was flushed on close, while the larger 512-byte write failed within the write function itself. The discrepancy stems from how the standard C library handles buffered I/O, particularly with `_IOFBF`, which leads to an unexpected write behavior when the buffer is larger than 512. The key is that `uploadFile` is a standard C library `FILE*`, not the direct file abstraction of the file system.


The initial hypothesis regarding buffered I/O being the source of the issue seemed incorrect, as the buffer size was not 0, contradicting the previous assumption. The `fwrite` returning 0 immediately on the first 512-byte write indicates an issue with the file opening or the SD card itself. A check revealed the target upload file `/uploads/Screenshot_20261114-111618_Chrome.jpg` was likely opened with `SD.open` in a way that causes the write to fail immediately.


The file open appears successful, confirming the prior issue wasn't directly related to opening. The HTTP POST request, specifically its multipart form-data structure, now demands scrutiny. Initial data received includes headers and boundary that the server-side multipart parser strips, leaving only the binary payload for writing. This immediately starts the data upload with the `UPLOAD_FILE_WRITE` status, and the size is now available.

The internal `sdTransaction` function uses SPI communication to send command packets to the SD card, and then receives a response token to determine card status. ```text
The file write operation is the likely point of failure. The initial assumption about the write operation was correct. Examining the previous interaction, the file upload began with a "UPLOAD START" instruction. The write operation attempted to write data to the specified destination.


The write operation's failure persists regardless of the buffer size (512 or 4096 bytes), which suggests the problem isn't directly related to buffer limits. The common denominator among all failing writes points towards a deeper issue in the underlying file system interaction, specifically with the `fwrite` function and its eventual call to the VFS driver. Further investigation is needed in the interaction between the VFS driver and the file system itself.


The `vfs_fat_write` function leverages Chan's FatFs library, specifically calling `f_write`. Examining Chan's `f_write` implementation is essential to understand the write process. The code's logic is being traced to identify the potential failure point during the write operation, specifically how it handles sector boundaries and cluster allocation.


The `f_write` function in Chan's FatFs library handles writes differently based on the remaining bytes to write (`btw`). When the byte count is less than a sector (512 bytes), direct sector writing is skipped; instead, data is copied to an internal sector buffer. The actual disk write via `disk_write` occurs only when the byte count is at least a full sector size, with `p` pointing to the buffer provided by the caller, which corresponds to the `uploadWriteBuffer`. This suggests a potential issue in how smaller writes are handled or buffered.
```

75: ## 3. Analysis & Key Insights
76: 
77: ### 3.1 Minimalist Dark Theme & Zero Curved Corners (`border-radius: 0`)
78: - **Visual Ergonomics**: Replaced intense multi-colored gradients and heavy blur backdrop filters with a solid, high-precision dark palette (`#0c0d11` body background, `#13151b` card backgrounds, `#181b22` input/table surfaces, `#272b35` borders).
79: - **Geometric Rigor**: Curved borders introduce unnecessary visual noise in high-density engineering dashboards. Setting `border-radius: 0 !important;` globally across cards, input elements, buttons (`.btn`, `.btn-upload`, `.btn-action`), badges, and progress bar containers enforces a crisp, modern architectural aesthetic.
80: 
81: ### 3.2 Removal of the "Active" Status Badge
82: - Previously, the dashboard header featured an animated blinking dot and text badge:
83:   ```html
84:   <span class="badge-online"><span class="badge-dot"></span> Online</span>
85:   ```
86: - Removing this element reduces header clutter and aligns the interface with modern minimalist design patterns. The right side of the header now cleanly hosts only the navigation action button (`[ 🌐 Static Site ]`).
87: 
88: ### 3.3 File Server HTML Placement & Static Asset Pipeline
89: - The file server interface was originally rendered purely via C++ PROGMEM strings in `include/html_templates.h`.
90: - By creating [`data/www/fileserver.html`](https://github.com/b1tranger/Microprocessor_Assembly_Lab/blob/main/Project.MM/LocalConfig/data/www/fileserver.html), developers can now directly view, edit, and preview the file server interface outside the microcontroller simulation.
91: - Running [`generate_assets.ps1`](https://github.com/b1tranger/Microprocessor_Assembly_Lab/blob/main/Project.MM/LocalConfig/scripts/generate_assets.ps1) automatically converts all files in `data/www/` into byte arrays in `include/default_assets.h`, ensuring the virtual FAT32 MicroSD card mounts with both `fileserver.html` and `index.html` write-protected under `/www/`.
92: 
93: ### 3.4 ESP32 C++ Core Firmware & PROGMEM Streaming Alignment
94: - The native ESP32 WebServer core streams dashboard pages in chunks via `server.sendContent(FPSTR(NAS_PAGE_HEADER))` to maintain a fixed ~2 KB RAM overhead.
95: - Keeping `include/html_templates.h` and [`data/www/fileserver.html`](https://github.com/b1tranger/Microprocessor_Assembly_Lab/blob/main/Project.MM/LocalConfig/data/www/fileserver.html) synchronized ensures that both the embedded live server and the local static HTML file produce identical visual experiences.
96: 
97: ### 3.6 Wokwi Virtual SD Card 256 MB Capacity Limit
98: - When loading `diagram.json`, the Wokwi VS Code extension validates `wokwi.toml` against its virtual disk creation schema.
99: - Specifying `size = "1G"` failed with `'size' must be at most 256 MB` because Wokwi's in-memory/simulated FAT formatting engine imposes a strict 256 MB maximum threshold.
100: - Adjusting to `size = "256M"` resolves the simulator configuration error while maintaining maximum allowable storage for files uploaded to `data/network/`.

151: ### 3.14 0-Byte Uploads & Aborted Multipart Stream Handling
152: - **Root Cause**:
153:   - In `handleFileUpload()`, on `UPLOAD_FILE_START`, the server opened the target file path via `SD.open(targetPath, FILE_WRITE)`. This created a directory entry on FAT32.
154:   - If a simulated network timeout, packet stall, or client abort occurred before the boundary finished, ESP32's `WebServer/src/Parsing.cpp` invoked `upload.status = UPLOAD_FILE_ABORTED`.
155:   - The previous handler only called `uploadFile.close()` without purging the file. This left an incomplete 0-byte file in `/uploads/` that was listed by `/api/files` and opened as corrupt by viewers.
156:   - Subsequent upload attempts failed to overwrite the stale cluster allocation properly.
157: - **Architectural Solution**:
158:   - Direct streaming I/O via `uploadFile.write(upload.buf, upload.currentSize)` bypassing manual double-buffering.
159:   - Added pre-upload sanitization: `if (SD.exists(currentUploadTarget)) SD.remove(currentUploadTarget);`.
160:   - Added abort auto-purge: on `UPLOAD_FILE_ABORTED`, `uploadFile.close()` is immediately followed by `SD.remove(currentUploadTarget)` to prevent incomplete 0-byte files from ever remaining on storage.
161:   - Enforced strict HTTP status validation on `/upload`: returns HTTP 500 JSON error if the file was aborted or wrote 0 bytes.
162: 
163: ### 3.15 Browser Loopback Transfer vs. Virtual SPI Storage Writing Lag
164: - **Why Upload Reaches 100% Immediately**:
165:   - When accessing `http://localhost:9080/`, traffic traverses the host loopback interface. The browser dumps the entire file payload into the local socket buffer in a few milliseconds, advancing `xhr.upload.onprogress` to 100%.
166: - **Why There Is a Subsequent Delay**:
167:   - The ESP32 in Wokwi is a cycle-accurate virtual simulation running Xtensa dual cores at ~20-50% real-time speed.
168:   - The firmware must consume packets through lwIP, parse multipart MIME boundaries, and bit-bang/SPI write each 512-byte block across GPIO 18/23/19 to FAT32.
169:   - Writing megabytes of data to virtual SD takes several seconds of CPU time. The browser waits for the HTTP 200 response during this interval.
170:   - Enhanced UI in `data/www/fileserver.html` to display a dedicated transition state at 100% (`Writing to Storage: <filename>`, `⚡ Committing...`, `⏱ Finalizing SD card write`) so users understand the server is committing data to storage.
171: 
172: ### 3.16 Network Self-Diagnostics Resource Contention & Stream Draining Fix
173: - **Diagnostic Output Trace**:
174:   - Test 1 (`/`): Response `200`
175:   - Test 2 (`/site`): Response `-11` (`HTTPC_ERROR_READ_TIMEOUT`)
176:   - Test 3 (`/get?file=lab_report.txt`): Response `-11` (`HTTPC_ERROR_READ_TIMEOUT`)
177:   - Test 4 (`/delete`): Response `-1` (`HTTPC_ERROR_CONNECTION_REFUSED`)
178:   - Test 5 (`/api/files`): Response `-1` (`HTTPC_ERROR_CONNECTION_REFUSED`)
179: - **Mechanism of Failure**:
180:   - Both `loopTask` (`server.handleClient()`) and `runClientTests` are pinned to Core 1 at priority 1.
181:   - In Test 1, `http.GET()` received `200 OK` from headers and called `http.end()` immediately without draining the 23 KB response body.
182:   - Closing a TCP socket with unread data in the receive buffer causes lwIP to issue a TCP RST (Reset).
183:   - The server's `server.streamFile()` was interrupted mid-stream on Core 1. Because there was 0 ms delay between tests, Test 2 fired while the server was still in error recovery, leading to successive 5-second timeouts (`-11`) and socket pool exhaustion (`-1`).
184:   - Serial monitor formatting had a staircase artifact because prints used `\n` without `\r`.
185: - **Architectural Solution**:

191: ### 3.17 Upload Partial Write Terminal Loop & 4KB Sector-Aligned SD Buffer
192: - **Terminal Trace**:
193:   - `[UPLOAD WARN] Partial write: 0 / 1436 bytes` repeating indefinitely on every incoming TCP packet.
194: - **Root Cause**:
195:   - VSPI clock was configured to 25 MHz (`25000000`). In Wokwi simulation, the virtual SD card component cannot reliably latch bulk sector writes at 25 MHz, causing block write timeouts or CRC errors (`FR_DISK_ERR` / `EIO`).
196:   - In standard C library file streaming, once `fwrite()` encounters a stream I/O error, the stream error flag is set (`ferror(_f) != 0`). Every subsequent call to `fwrite()` immediately fails and returns 0 without attempting I/O.
197:   - Writing raw 1,436-byte network chunks unbuffered forced partial-sector read-modify-write operations across 512-byte FAT32 boundaries.
198:   - Filenames containing apostrophes (`'`) like `The Regressed Mercenary's Machinations` posed directory entry formatting collisions.
199:   - Bare `\n` in `Serial.printf` caused staircase indentation in serial consoles.
200: - **Architectural Solution**:
201:   - Reverted `SD.begin()` from 25 MHz to standard reliable 4 MHz (`4000000`).
202:   - Implemented 4,096-byte sector-aligned buffer (`uploadWriteBuffer[4096]`), accumulating 1,436-byte network chunks and flushing exclusively in 8-sector (4 KB) aligned blocks.
203:   - Added `uploadWriteError` circuit breaker: halts further disk writes immediately on the first error, logs once, and safely purges the incomplete file, eliminating terminal spam.
